article.title: Jev Engineering: Parallel Decisions for a 300-Agent Kimi Swarm

blocks.text: Your swarm returns 300 results at once. Then something reviews them one by one. That review line is a queue hiding inside a parallel system, and it quietly gives back the speed you paid for. Here is how to judge all 300 in a single pass.
300 Kimi results at once        1 Jev pass to judge them       0 review queue
Kimi finishes 300 tasks in parallel. Then your pipeline checks them in single file.

A Kimi swarm is built to fan out. Point it at a hundred companies, three hundred sources, or a full codebase and it comes back with hundreds of results in the time a single agent would finish one. The execution is parallel from end to end.

Then comes the part nobody draws on the architecture diagram: somebody has to decide what to do with each result. Keep it or requeue it. Trust it or flag it. Send it to the report or throw it out. In most setups that judgment runs through a large model, one result per call, 300 calls in a row. The swarm sprinted. The review walks.
Jev, the decision model from TypeSafe AI, is built for exactly this kind of work: short, typed judgments over structured input. And it can take the whole set in one request instead of three hundred.
Kimi produces 300 results at once → Jev judges all 300 at once → the pipeline never slows to single file.
STEP 01
Find the review line in your pipeline

Look at what happens after the swarm returns. If there is a loop that walks the results and asks a model something about each one, you have found it. That loop is serial, and its length is the size of your swarm. At 10 agents it is a small delay. At 300 it becomes the longest stage in the whole run.

The irony is that each individual judgment is tiny. "Is this revenue figure consistent with its source?" is a one-word answer. You are not waiting on hard thinking. You are waiting on 300 separate trips to ask easy questions.

It also hides well. Nobody writes "a review loop that takes longer than the swarm" into a design doc. It grows on its own: first a quick sanity check, then a relevance filter, then a source check, each added one line at a time, each running once per result. By the time the swarm is at 300 agents, the checks behind it have quietly become the longest part of every run.
STEP 02
Check that the judgments stand alone

Batching works when each judgment only needs its own result and the shared context. Result #041 can be scored without knowing how #042 scored. That independence is what lets you hand Jev the whole set at once.

A few judgments do depend on each other, and those have to stay in order. Ranking the top 10 needs every score first. Picking the best duplicate needs all duplicates found first. The practical pattern is two stages: score everything independently in one pass, then run the few comparative decisions on the scored set.

This split is the whole design, and it is worth being strict about it. The moment a stage-one question starts looking at other results, "is this better than #040?", it stops being independent and drags the whole batch back into order. Keep stage one about each result on its own terms: does it match its source, is it on topic, is it complete. Everything relative waits for stage two, where it runs once over a set that is already scored.
STEP 03
Judge the whole set in one Jev call

Stage one becomes a single request. You send Jev the shared context once, the list of Kimi results, and one question applied to each. It returns a typed verdict per result with a confidence score, and the results split cleanly into keep and requeue.
The shared context is sent once, not 300 times. That alone cuts the input you pay for, because a sequential loop repeats the same brief, the same rules and the same schema in every single call.

What comes back is not a wall of prose to read. It is a map of the run: one verdict per result, every one typed, every one with a confidence you can threshold. You can see at a glance where the swarm was solid and where it needs another pass.
STEP 04
Ask ahead with speculative branches

The second move removes waiting you did not know you had. When the next step of the run can go several ways, ask Jev about every branch in the same pass, before you know which one you will take. When the branch resolves, the decision is already sitting there.

Two of the three answers get thrown away, and that is fine. At decision pricing the discarded answers cost almost nothing, while the time saved is a full round trip on every turn. In a Kimi run that turns thousands of times, that difference adds up.

The same trick works inside the review itself. If the next move depends on how many results fail, you can ask, in the same pass, what to do if the failure rate is low, moderate, or high. When the verdicts land, the plan for each case is already there, and the run continues without stopping to ask.
STEP 05
Measure the trips, not just the tokens

The saving shows up in round trips. Reviewing 300 results one by one is 300 requests, each with its own network wait and its own copy of the shared context. Chunking into groups of 30 gets you to 10. A single pass gets you to one.

Because the review now runs on Jev at $0.042 per million input tokens, and the context is sent once instead of 300 times, the review stage stops being the slowest and most repetitive part of a Kimi run.

Chunking is a reasonable middle ground when a set is very large or a single request would be unwieldy. Ten requests instead of three hundred already removes most of the waiting. The point is not the number one. It is that the count of review calls should stop growing with the size of the swarm.
STEP 06
Close the loop: only the misses go back

A review that runs in one pass unlocks a cleaner loop around the whole swarm. Kimi runs everything, Jev judges everything in one pass, and only the results that failed go back for another run. Then the misses get judged again, in one pass, and the smaller set of remaining misses goes back again.

Each round is smaller than the last. The first pass reviews 300. The second reviews the 29 that failed. The third reviews the handful still left. Because every round is a single Jev call, the loop costs a few requests in total, and it stops on its own once nothing fails.

Without the single-pass review, this loop is painful: each round means another long line of calls, so teams run it once and ship whatever the first pass produced. With it, running a second and third round is cheap enough to be the default.
Match the review to the swarm

A Kimi swarm changed the shape of execution: not one task at a time, but hundreds at once. Most pipelines never changed the shape of the review that follows it, so the fastest stage feeds straight into the slowest one.
Jev fixes the mismatch by giving the review the same shape as the work. Four habits cover most of it:
Split the review into two stages. Independent verdicts first, comparisons after.
Send stage one as one pass. Shared context once, one typed verdict per result.
Ask about upcoming branches early. The answers you discard are cheaper than the wait.
Send back only the misses. Each round is smaller, and each round is still one pass.
If 300 agents can finish at the same moment, 300 verdicts can arrive at the same moment too.

data.markdown:
```python
python · review.py
results = kimi.run(plan)              # 300 results, in parallel

# one pass: shared context once, one verdict per result
verdicts = jev.batch(context, [
  noul(f"does {r.id} match its source?") for r in results
])

keep    = [r for r, v in zip(results, verdicts) if v >= 0.85]
requeue = [r for r, v in zip(results, verdicts) if v <  0.85]
kimi.rerun(requeue)                      # only the misses go back
```

```python
python · loop.py
pending = kimi.run(plan)                   # round 1: all 300
while pending:
    v = jev.batch(context, [noul(f"{r.id} ok?") for r in pending])
    keep(r for r, s in zip(pending, v) if s >= 0.85)
    misses  = [r for r, s in zip(pending, v) if s < 0.85]
    pending = kimi.rerun(misses) if misses else []   # smaller each round
```
